newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu rules out settlement halt.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu rules out settlement halt.

text.p: Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu said on Tuesday he hoped Egypt could broker a resumption of peace talks with Palestinians.
But the prime minister rejected a key PLO demand for a freeze on Jewish settlement including the controversial Har Homa construction on occupied land on the outskirts of Jerusalem.

"I am certainly willing to try all avenues even against some advice that I received," Netanyahu said of Egypt's mediation attempt. "There is hope, I hope that it succeeds," he told Reuters in a television interview.

Israeli and Palestinian negotiators are due to meet in Israel on Thursday in an attempt to break a two-month-old deadlock caused by Netanyahu's decision to break ground at Har Homa, Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic.
Both sides have played down expectations of a breakthrough but the United States and European Union are behind the Egyptian initiative.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat has been pressing for a three to six-month halt in settlement building to allow talks on a final resolution of the Israel-Palestinian conflict to restart.
Netanyahu ruled this out, dismissing settlement as a non-issue.

But he acknowledged that Israel would not be able to hold on to all the West Bank land that it caputured in 1967. As part of a campaign to wean settlers and other right-wing nationalists off the dream of a Greater Israel, officials leaked a map showing which parts of the West Bank would be ceded to Palestinians under a final settlement by 1999.

"We have to adjust our expectations to reality. I have put forward proposals both on how to enter accelerated negotiations for a final settlement and what the shape of that settlement could look like," Netanyahu said, insisting he was honouring the 1993 Oslo peace accord that he inherited from a centre-left Labour government one year ago.
"You know the great work that I myself have done trying to achieve a consensus in the Israeli public which naturally means a really painful adjustment to reality," he said.

"Both sides have to have their ideology adjusted to the facts on the ground. We have done that and we are doing it but I think equally there has to be an adjustment of the Palestinian ideological goals to reality. Arafat has to stop talking about a return to the '67 lines," Netanyahu said.
He said PLO leaders should tell their people: "We are not going to get it all".
He dismissed charges that he had undermined Israel's chance of a broad peace with the Arab world by giving in to the right wing.
"I am pro-Oslo. I am for keeping agreements, not because I fell in love with Oslo, I thought it was a flawed agreement, but agreements should be kept."
"We see on the one hand Israel fulfills Oslo and is not credited for it, and the Palestinian Authority is violating Oslo but is credited with keeping it," he said.
